outline.chapter_title: The Limitations of Tokenization in Large Language Models
outline.description: This chapter introduces the foundational problems with the current standard of NLP: subword tokenization. It sets the stage for why byte-level modeling is a necessary evolution for robust and efficient AI.
subtopics: The Mechanism of Subword Tokenization (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding)
Bias and Inequities: Domain sensitivity, modality sensitivity, and multilingual inequity
The Orthographic Knowledge Gap: Why tokens fail at character-level understanding
Sensitivity to Input Noise and Out-of-Vocabulary issues
The Computational Trade-off: Why we don't simply train on raw bytes (Sequence length vs. Transformer costs)

outline.chapter_title: From Bytes to Patches: Dynamic Data Segmentation
outline.description: This chapter explores the core conceptual shift from fixed-vocabulary tokens to dynamic, learnable 'patches.' It covers different methods of grouping bytes to balance compute and information density.
subtopics: Defining Patching: The mapping of bytes to latent representations
Static Patching: Strided Patching (K-bytes) and its limitations
Heuristic Patching: Space Patching and linguistic boundaries
Entropy Patching: Using a small Byte LM to identify high-uncertainty boundaries
The Property of Incremental Patching vs. BPE
The Patch Size vs. Computation relationship: How patch size controls FLOPs

outline.description: A deep dive into the technical architecture of the BLT. This chapter explains the three-part system consisting of local encoders, a global latent transformer, and a local decoder.
subtopics: The High-Level Architecture Overview
The Latent Global Transformer: Processing high-level latent representations
The Local Encoder: Byte-to-Patch mapping
Encoder Hash n-gram Embeddings: Capturing local context with RollPolyHash
Multi-Headed Cross-Attention: Pooling byte representations into patches
The Local Decoder: Patch-to-Byte reconstruction
Decoder Cross-Attention: Reversing the query/key roles for byte generation

outline.description: This chapter details the experimental methodology, including how the researchers measured 'FLOP-controlled' performance and the significant findings regarding model scaling.
subtopics: Defining Training FLOPs for Byte-Level Models
Bits-Per-Byte (BPB): A tokenizer-independent metric for perplexity
Compute-Optimal Scaling: Comparing BLT with Llama 3
The 'Patches Scale Better Than Tokens' Hypothesis
Trading Inference Flops for Model Size: Simultaneous scaling of patches and parameters
Experimental Setup: Data mixtures (Llama 2 and BLT-1T datasets)

outline.description: This chapter highlights the qualitative and quantitative advantages of byte-level modeling over tokenization, specifically in handling noise and specialized tasks.
subtopics: Robustness to Input Noise: Testing with AntSpeak, Drop, and RandomCase
Phonology: Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) task performance
The CUTE Benchmark: Character manipulation and orthographic similarity
Low-Resource Machine Translation: Generalizing to long-tail byte sequences
Byte-ifying Pre-trained Models: Distilling knowledge from Llama 3.1 into a BLT framework

outline.description: The final chapter analyzes the specific components that make BLT successful and discusses the remaining challenges for the field of byte-level modeling.
subtopics: Ablating Patching Schemes: Entropy vs. Space vs. Strided
The Necessity of Cross-Attention and Hash n-gram Embeddings
Impact of Entropy Model Hyperparameters (Size and Context Window)
Current Limitations: Wall-clock time vs. FLOP parity
Future Directions: End-to-end learnable patching and larger-scale byte models
